inputs.need:
I direct the clinical skills centre at a medical school with 180 students per year. Second-year students get eight faculty-led sessions on examination skills before their first OSCE, taught by clinicians who are paid sessional rates and are increasingly hard to book. For two years we have also run optional near-peer sessions in which trained final-year students teach small groups of second-years, and the student feedback is very positive. The dean has asked whether we could replace half of the faculty-led sessions with near-peer sessions from next year.

I would like to do a cost-effectiveness analysis of that change before we commit. Costs on our side are faculty sessional fees, tutor training and small payments to near-peer tutors, room bookings and simulated patients. The main effect we care about is whether second-years pass the examination skills stations of the OSCE at the first attempt; we also hear that tutors themselves learn a lot, and some faculty worry that near-peer tutors teach shortcuts. We have OSCE station scores for the last four years, attendance registers for both kinds of session since 2024, and the finance office can give us sessional fees.

I need help with how to compare the options fairly when students chose whether to attend the near-peer sessions, what outcome to use as the effect measure, which expenses to include and from whose perspective, and how many years of students we need before a result means anything. Nobody is funding this; it has to be done with existing data and a small amount of my own and an education fellow's time.
inputs.constraints: No funding. Existing data only, plus about 4 hours per week of the director's and an education fellow's time from October 2026 to May 2027. Student data may be used only in de-identified form under the school's education data policy.

records.title: Near-peer versus faculty teaching of clinical examination skills: a randomised comparison of OSCE performance
records.authors: Okoro-Lindberg F, Delacroix-Mensah P, Watanabe-Hurst G
records.abstract: We randomly allocated 124 second-year medical students to four examination-skills sessions taught either by trained final-year students or by faculty clinicians. The outcome was performance on four examination stations of the end-of-year OSCE, marked by examiners unaware of allocation. Station pass rates were 88 percent after near-peer teaching and 86 percent after faculty teaching, and the mean station score difference was 0.9 points in favour of near-peer teaching (95 percent CI -1.8 to 3.6). Students rated both formats highly, and near-peer tutors reported more confidence in their own examination technique. The study was at one school and too small to show a difference of less than 10 percentage points in pass rates.

records.title: Near-peer teaching in undergraduate medical education: a systematic review of learner and tutor outcomes
records.authors: Harrow-Adeyemi S, Kristensen-Obi T, Mahlaba-Ruiz C, Petersen-Kaur A
records.abstract: We searched four databases to 2020 for studies comparing near-peer with faculty teaching in undergraduate medicine. We included 32 studies, of which 7 were randomised. Most studies reported similar or better learner performance after near-peer teaching, but outcomes were heterogeneous and usually measured immediately after teaching. Learner satisfaction was high in almost all studies. Tutors reported gains in knowledge and teaching skills. Only 4 studies reported costs, and none valued the time of student tutors. The review concludes that near-peer teaching is at least comparable for skills teaching but that economic evidence is sparse.

records.title: Costs of near-peer and faculty-led clinical skills teaching at one medical school: a cost comparison
records.abstract: We costed one academic year of examination-skills teaching at a medical school from the school's perspective. Faculty-led teaching cost 46 currency units per student contact hour, mainly sessional fees, and near-peer teaching cost 11 units per student contact hour, including tutor training, tutor payments and supervision. When the time of student tutors was valued at the rate paid for research assistant work, the near-peer cost rose to 19 units. Room and simulated patient charges were the same for both formats. The analysis did not measure learning outcomes, so it cannot say whether the cheaper option was equally effective.

records.title: Self-selection into optional near-peer sessions and OSCE results: an analysis of three student years
records.authors: Achebe-Lindqvist M, Farrow-Nakamura J, Osei-Brandt L
records.abstract: We examined 510 students across three years in which near-peer examination-skills sessions were optional. Students who attended had higher first-year assessment scores than those who did not. The unadjusted difference in OSCE examination-station scores between attenders and non-attenders was 5.2 points, which shrank to 1.1 points after adjustment for first-year scores and sex. Attendance was lowest among students who commuted long distances. The authors caution that comparisons based on optional attendance mainly reflect who chooses to attend, and recommend allocation by timetable or randomisation for future evaluations.

records.title: What final-year tutors gain from near-peer teaching: an interview study
records.venue: Journal of Peer Learning in Medicine
records.abstract: We interviewed 18 final-year medical students who had tutored second-years in examination skills. Tutors described consolidating their own knowledge, learning to give feedback and growing confidence in front of groups. Several described time pressure in the months before their final examinations and asked for sessions to be scheduled earlier in the year. Some tutors felt unsure how far to correct technique that differed from what faculty had taught them. The authors recommend a short training course, a teaching guide aligned with faculty expectations and a limit on tutoring hours before finals.

records.title: Detection of examination technique errors by near-peer and faculty tutors: an observational comparison
records.authors: Varga-Okonjo T, Lindgren-Assefa H, Brooks-Ishikawa N
records.abstract: We video-recorded 60 small-group examination-skills sessions, 30 led by near-peer tutors and 30 by faculty, and compared the errors in student technique that tutors corrected with those identified by two independent reviewers. Near-peer tutors left 22 percent of technique errors uncorrected compared with 12 percent for faculty tutors. The difference was largest for cardiovascular and neurological examinations. After a one-hour calibration session for tutors, the proportion of errors missed by near-peer tutors fell to 15 percent. Sessions were at one school and tutors knew they were being recorded.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One small randomised comparison and a review of 32 studies suggest that near-peer teaching of examination skills gives similar results to faculty teaching, but they cannot exclude small differences. A single-school costing shows near-peer teaching is much cheaper per contact hour, less so when tutor time is valued. Comparisons based on optional attendance are dominated by self-selection. Near-peer tutors miss more technique errors, which a short calibration session reduces. The evidence supports an economic evaluation with a fair comparison of groups and explicit valuation of tutor time.
response.gradeRationale: One small randomised study and a heterogeneous review for effect, single-school observational costing, and confounded attendance data; direction consistent but imprecise and indirect.

response.rationale: The question is whether a cheaper teaching format keeps performance, which is an economic evaluation. Two candidate designs were weighed: an analysis of the historical years with optional attendance, and a concurrent comparison in 2027 with tutorial groups allocated to the formats by timetable block. The historical option is refused because self-selection dominates optional attendance (c3). The concurrent comparison supplies a fair effect; the costing approach follows the retrieved costing record, with tutor time valued in sensitivity analysis (c2), and the effect is framed around similar pass rates (c1).

response.designSummary: Cost-effectiveness analysis alongside a comparison of tutorial groups allocated by timetable block; clustering by tutorial group.
response.sampleSize: One class of about 180 students gives about 90 per arm. With pass rates near 87 percent, a 95 percent interval for the difference in pass proportions is about 10 percentage points either side of the estimate before allowing for clustering, so one year cannot show non-inferiority within a 5-point margin; that would need about 700 students per arm. The analysis therefore reports the probability that the near-peer option is cost-effective at stated values per additional student passing, and plans to add the 2028 class before any firm conclusion.
response.primaryAnalysis: Difference in first-attempt pass proportion between arms from a mixed-effects logistic model with tutorial group as a random effect and first-year assessment score as a covariate; incremental cost per student; non-parametric bootstrap of 5,000 resamples by tutorial group for the joint distribution of cost and effect; cost-effectiveness acceptability curve.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Sensitivity analyses valuing tutor time at the research assistant rate and at zero, and excluding calibration costs; faculty hours released.
response.missingData: Students who do not sit the May OSCE are reported by arm; the primary analysis includes students who sat it, with a sensitivity analysis counting absentees as not passing.

response.title: Replacing half of faculty-led examination-skills teaching with near-peer sessions: a cost-effectiveness analysis alongside a concurrent comparison
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the incremental cost per additional student passing all examination-skills stations when four of eight faculty sessions are replaced by calibrated near-peer sessions. Design: cost-effectiveness analysis alongside allocation of 2027 tutorial groups by timetable block, school perspective. Results and conclusions will follow the May 2027 OSCE.
response.introduction: Near-peer teaching gives similar short-term performance in small studies and is cheaper per contact hour, but economic evaluations with fair comparisons are rare.
response.methods: Eighteen tutorial groups are allocated by timetable block. The effect measure is first-attempt pass on all examination-skills stations; costs come from finance records. Uncertainty is shown by bootstrap and acceptability curves.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present costs, pass proportions, the incremental ratio and acceptability curves.
response.discussion: The discussion will set the result against the retrieved randomised comparison and costing, and state what a second year of data would add.
response.limitations: One school, one year, allocation by timetable rather than randomisation, and imprecise effect estimates.
